displayQuote: Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine

meta.title: Who really said "Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Marx never wrote it. His 1866 letter to François Lafargue credits “old Luther”: a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it under Misattributed. Marx wrote, in 1866, that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything — crediting Luther.

answer.label: Marx — but not in these words, and not about trust
answer.sourceLine: Marx wrote no such sentence. Thanking a correspondent in Bordeaux for a gift of wine on 12 November 1866, he wrote that he inclined “somewhat to old Luther’s view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything” — and then added, in the same breath, “(There are exceptions to every rule.)” The letter survives in full ↗. The popular line swaps worthlessness for untrustworthiness, drops Luther, and drops the exception; Wikiquote lists it as misattributed ↗.

source.heading: The letter it was rewritten from

docMeta.dd: Letter to François Lafargue in Bordeaux
English text as printed in Marx/Engels Collected Works, vol. 42, p. 334

source.excerpt: My sincere thanks for the wine. Being myself from a winegrowing region, and former owner of a vineyard, I know a good wine when I come across one. I even incline somewhat to old Luther’s view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything. (There are exceptions to every rule.) But one cannot, for example, deny that the political movement in England has been spurred on by the commercial treaty with France and the import of French wines.
trail: Wikiquote files the popular sentence under Misattributed on its Karl Marx page ↗ — and, unusually for that section, names a real document behind it: a letter to François Lafargue in Bordeaux, 12 November 1866, as published in Marx/Engels Collected Works, vol. 42, p. 334.

That letter survives complete. Writing from London to thank Lafargue for a gift of wine, Marx says: “Being myself from a winegrowing region, and former owner of a vineyard, I know a good wine when I come across one. I even incline somewhat to old Luther’s view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything. (There are exceptions to every rule.)” — the complete text, with its MECW volume and page ↗.

Marx did not present the thought as his own, and the man he credited probably never said it either: the proverb “Who loves not wine, women and song, remains a fool his whole life long” is often erroneously attributed to Martin Luther and first appears in print in 1775 ↗.

The English text is hard to reach at its usual address. The Marxists Internet Archive deleted every text taken from the Collected Works on 30 April 2014 ↗, at the direction of Lawrence & Wishart, who hold the copyright — so the link Wikiquote still cites now serves a copyright notice rather than the letter.
source.excerptNote: The paraphrase keeps the wine and drops everything that qualifies it: the credit to Luther, the actual subject (a man’s worth, not his honesty), and Marx’s own parenthesis.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be assigned to the popular sentence, because it has no identifiable author, work or date — it is an anonymous rewrite. The letter behind it is a separate question: Marx wrote it in French in 1866 and it was first published in Annali (Milan) in 1958, while the English wording quoted here is the translation printed in the Marx/Engels Collected Works, whose copyright Lawrence & Wishart hold — which is why the Marxists Internet Archive removed all MECW material from its site on 30 April 2014 ↗.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.heading: About Karl Marx
author.bio: Karl Marx was deep in the manuscript that would become Das Kapital when he broke off to write this thank-you note — he blames the book, and recurring illness, for months of unanswered post. He had been born in Trier in 1818, in the Mosel wine country, into a family that owned two small vineyards, and the wine talk in his letters is the talk of someone who grew up around it rather than a man reaching for a metaphor. What he did not do, here or anywhere else, was tell anyone to distrust a person who does not like wine.

cite.sourceCitation: Karl Marx to François Lafargue, London, 12 November 1866, in Marx/Engels Collected Works, vol. 42, p. 334; written in French and first published in Annali (Milan, 1958). The English sentence “Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine” appears in no work or letter of Marx’s and is listed as misattributed by Wikiquote.

copyAttribution: Karl Marx never wrote "Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine." What he wrote, to François Lafargue on 12 November 1866, was: "I even incline somewhat to old Luther's view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything. (There are exceptions to every rule.)" — Marx/Engels Collected Works, vol. 42, p. 334. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What happened to it
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual. Most quotes pinned on Marx are inventions with nothing underneath them; this one has a real sentence underneath, rewritten far enough to say something he did not say.

items.who: Nobody — it has no traceable author
items.why: Quote sites print the sentence bare. The AZQuotes entry ↗ carries Marx’s name and a row of topic tags — wine, food, drinking — and no book, letter, date or page at all. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed ↗.

items.who: Marx credited it to Martin Luther
items.why: The letter does not offer the thought as Marx’s own: he says he inclines “somewhat to old Luther’s view” — see the letter ↗. Wikiquote reads the line as a restating of the “wine, women and song” proverb then attributed to Luther. That attribution does not hold either: the proverb first appears in print in 1775 ↗, more than two centuries after the 1536 table talk in which Luther said something loosely comparable.

items.who: Marx — but he was judging a man’s worth, not his honesty
items.why: “A man who does not love wine will never be good for anything” is a verdict on usefulness; “be careful to trust” turns it into a warning about character. The rewrite also loses what Marx wrote in the very next breath — “(There are exceptions to every rule.)” ↗

misattribution.truthLine: What Marx actually wrote, in French, from London on 12 November 1866: “I even incline somewhat to old Luther’s view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything. (There are exceptions to every rule.)” — letter to François Lafargue, Marx/Engels Collected Works, vol. 42, p. 334 ↗

context.heading: A thank-you note that turned political
lead: The setting is domestic, not doctrinal. Marx was writing to François Lafargue in Bordeaux — the father of Paul Lafargue, who married Marx’s daughter Laura at St Pancras registry office in April 1868 ↗ — to apologise for months of silence and to thank him for a gift of wine. The credentials Marx offers are real ones: he was born in Trier in 1818, in Riesling country, and The World of Fine Wine notes that his family owned two small vineyards along the Ruwer at Mertesdorf ↗. “Former owner of a vineyard” is not a flourish.

Then, in the same paragraph, the letter swerves. Cheap French wine, Marx argues, had done English politics some good: the commercial treaty with France and the wine imports it brought had spurred the political movement along — one of the few useful things Louis Bonaparte managed, bought at the price of general demoralisation. The rest of the letter is a father-in-law-to-be at work: chasing missing paperwork for Paul’s application to the College of Surgeons, and asking François to tell his son to desist from propaganda in Paris, because “this is a dangerous time” and he would be the better fighter for holding himself in check.
context.detailsSummary: Two shapes of the paraphrase, and who traced it first
detailsBody: The rewrite circulates in two forms. Quote sites give “Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine” — which, read literally, advises the opposite of what it means. The World of Fine Wine opens its essay on Marx, Engels and wine ↗ with the grammatically repaired version, “Be careful of trusting a person who does not like wine” — and then, further down, quotes the real letter. Neither wording is in it.

The trail back to the letter was walked in public. A thread on the Marxism mailing list ↗ asked where the wine line came from, and a participant produced the November 1866 passage — the same source Wikiquote now cites. Quote Investigator, which has looked into several sayings pinned on Marx, has no article on this one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists "Be careful to trust a person who does not like wine" in its Misattributed section, noting it was written in a letter to Francois Lafargue in Bordeaux, 12 November 1866, as published in MECW Volume 42, p. 334, as "That a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything."

Same page fetched as raw wikitext to defeat truncation: the line sits at L844-845, inside the ==Misattributed== section (which opens at L823) and before ==Quotes about Marx== (L849), with the MECW vol. 42 p. 334 note and a link to the marxists.org letter URL.

Full English text of Marx's 12 November 1866 letter to François Lafargue in Bordeaux, containing "Being myself from a winegrowing region, and former owner of a vineyard, I know a good wine when I come across one. I even incline somewhat to old Luther's view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything. (There are exceptions to every rule.)", plus the wine-and-commercial-treaty passage, the College of Surgeons paperwork, and the request that Paul desist from propaganda in Paris; the header source note reads "Marx-Engels Collected Works, Volume 42, p. 334; First published: in the language of the original, French, in Annali, Milano, 1958".

Marxists Internet Archive notice: "Lawrence & Wishart, who hold the copyright for the Marx Engels Collected Works, have directed Marxists Internet Archive to delete all texts originating from MECW. Accordingly, from 30th April 2014, no material from MECW is available from marxists.org."

CHECKED AND FAILED — deliberately not used as a page link. The URL Wikiquote cites for the letter returns 302 Found and redirects to the MECW removal notice; it does not serve the letter or the quoted sentence.

"The proverb 'Who loves not wine, women and song, remains a fool his whole life long' is often erroneously attributed to Martin Luther, and appears in print for the first time in 1775"; the article also cites Luther's 1536 table talk as the nearest comparable remark, and dates the bare phrase "Wein, Weib und Gesang" to a German folksong of 1602.

The essay opens with the popular paraphrase in the form "Be careful of trusting a person who does not like wine", then quotes the genuine letter lines "Being myself from a wine-growing region and former owner of a vineyard, I know a good wine when I come across one" and "I even incline somewhat to old Luther's view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything"; it states Marx was born in Trier and that his family owned two small vineyards along the Ruwer in Mertesdorf.
The AZQuotes entry for this quote shows only Marx's name and topic tags (Wine, Food, Be Careful, Drinking) — no book, letter, date, page or citation of any kind.

A Marxism mailing-list thread asking for the source of the Marx wine quote, in which a participant supplies the November 1866 letter to François Lafargue and the wording "I even incline somewhat to old Luther's view that a man who does not love wine will never be good for anything."

Wikipedia gives Karl Marx's birth as 5 May 1818 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia, and his death as 14 March 1883 in London, describing him as a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist.
Wikipedia states that Paul Lafargue married (Laura Marx) at St Pancras registry office in April 1868.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quote — a site search for "love wine" returns "Nothing Found". Recorded as a negative check; deliberately not used as a page link.
